column25: Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 as close substitutes expand. Each price experiment moves along its own demand curve, while the comparison shows changed responsiveness across periods.
column27: Using the stated percentage responses, |Ed| changes from 4/10=0.4 to 16/10=1.6. Each price change causes movement along the demand curve applicable then. column11: LO1.3
column16: Ignoring opportunity cost, counting sunk expense, or comparing total rather than incremental profit.
column18: A training firm must decide whether to accept one additional client. A nonrefundable $4,000 license fee is already paid, and existing contracts will earn $50,000 profit either way. The new client will pay $18,000 with probability 0.75 and $10,000 otherwise. Service costs $11,000, support costs $2,000, and using the specialists forgoes another job's $4,000 net profit. All figures concern the firm; there are no other effects. Which marginal decision maximizes expected profit?
column19: Reject: relevant expected marginal profit is -$1,000.
column20: Accept: relevant expected marginal profit is +$3,000.
column21: Reject: relevant expected marginal profit is -$5,000.
column22: Accept: relevant expected marginal profit is +$49,000.
column25: Reject: relevant expected marginal profit is -$1,000.
column27: Expected marginal revenue is 0.75 × $18,000 + 0.25 × $10,000 = $16,000. Relevant marginal cost is $11,000 + $2,000 + $4,000 = $17,000, so accepting lowers expected profit by $1,000. The paid license fee is sunk and the $50,000 from existing contracts is unchanged. Omitting the forgone job, adding the sunk fee, or including existing profit gives the distractor results.

column18: A hospital evaluates all benefits and costs using the same points scale. One treatment provides 88 benefit points and has a 42-point supply cost. column11: LO1.3
column16: Using a blanket rule without checking whether the cost is truly sunk.
column18: A fee has already been paid, but its refund terms have not yet been checked. When should it affect the current decision?
column19: Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
column20: Only when total benefits are positive.
column21: Always, because past spending must be recovered.
column22: Never, even if a refund remains available.
column25: Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
column27: Check whether the current choice changes how much of the fee can be recovered. A refund available under one choice but not another is relevant; a payment that cannot be recovered or changed is sunk. Having paid the fee does not by itself establish that it is irrelevant, and a desire to recover past spending is not a marginal benefit.

column22: Hire only the worker adding 14 parcels because lower marginal product means lower marginal labor cost.
column25: Hire the worker adding 22 parcels but not the one adding 14; their added revenues are $132 and $84 even though both have positive marginal product.
column27: Compare added revenue with the $100 wage. 22×$6=$132 exceeds the wage; 14×$6=$84 does not. Diminishing marginal product need not mean negative marginal product or immediate unprofitability.
